1.title: Collaborative
1.summary:
The collaborative option involves you and {partner_name} sitting in the same room to discuss your situation and explore solutions. But you would not be alone. You and {partner_name} would each have your own specially trained lawyer (collaborative lawyers) to help you in the discussions.

The lawyers will work together to ensure the discussions are open and constructive. You and {partner_name} share a positive commitment, recorded in writing, to avoid court. Third party specialists such as financial advisers or counsellors can be brought in to assist the discussions. All the work will be done in the meetings – the collaborative lawyers will avoid sending letters or emails to each other as this can lead to misunderstandings or upset feelings. Your collaborative lawyer will make sure you are protected but will work together with the collaborative lawyer for {partner_name} to look after the interests of the whole family, especially any children.

Fortunately, collaborative lawyers are legally trained so their experience should assist you and {partner_name}. It appears from your answers that your circumstances are relatively straightforward.

collaborative.affordability:
Collaborative law is a structured, lawyer-supported process that helps you and {partner_name} resolve matters without going to court. You each have a specially trained collaborative lawyer present at joint meetings, providing real-time legal advice and supporting practical, family-focused solutions. Costs mainly relate to meeting time, with minimal correspondence to keep fees controlled. Additional experts are used only by agreement, and if settlement is reached, your lawyers prepare the legally binding paperwork.

Collaborative law is more affordable than court, where costs can escalate rapidly, and you retain control over timing and outcomes. While more expensive than basic mediation, it offers greater legal protection and can reduce the risk of failed mediation, escalating conflict, and increased costs. Legal Aid is not available so costs are usually self-funded, though short-term support from family, friends, or a financial contribution from {partner_name} may be possible.

1.title: Court
1.summary:
The court option involves a judge, who will control the steps to be taken by you and {partner_name}.

If you cannot reach agreement you will have a final hearing (or trial) where a judge will give a binding decision. Some people are represented by lawyers and some people conduct the proceedings themselves. The court option is appropriate when all other options have been exhausted. Court will give you the certainty of a final decision but you may find it costly and stressful.

court.affordability:
In the court process, you pay for a judge to make a binding decision if you and {partner_name} cannot agree. Most people also incur solicitor’s fees to prepare documents, manage deadlines, and represent them at hearings. While some represent themselves to reduce costs, this can be stressful and challenging without legal expertise. Court cases typically involve extensive preparation, multiple hearings, and ongoing legal work, all of which increase expense.

Court is generally the most expensive, slowest, and most stressful way to resolve a family dispute. Costs often escalate due to delay, repeated hearings, and adversarial procedures. Although it provides finality, it is usually treated as a last resort, except where safety or power imbalance makes other options unsuitable.

Legal Aid is only available in very limited circumstances so costs are usually self-funded. If finances are tight, you may seek financial support from family or friends. Litigation loans may be available.

You will have to work together to identify the issues that need to be resolved. You will need to negotiate with each other to settle any differences you may have. At various points you may wish to check with a lawyer that you are on the right track or ask a lawyer to draft any agreement you reach into a consent order for approval by the court.

However, without any legal advice, there is a risk that an informal agreement could later prove unfair or unenforceable, potentially leading to future disputes.

Any legal advice is usually self-funded, as Legal Aid (for preliminary advice or to draft a consent order) is rarely available.

1.title: Early Neutral Evaluation
1.summary:
Early Neutral Evaluation involves you and {partner_name} agreeing that you will ask an impartial family law professional (like a senior lawyer) how a Judge would deal with your dispute if you were in court.

This neutral evaluation can be delivered in person or in writing. A neutral evaluator can deal with financial disputes and with disagreements over your children. Unlike the family court, you and {partner_name} would be able to choose the neutral evaluator as well as the date and location of the evaluation. This can be arranged much more quickly than a court hearing and is less expensive. The neutral evaluator cannot provide a binding decision for you and {partner_name} but it will help to focus your mind. It is a good option to consider if you cannot agree an issue with {partner_name} and you are anxious that the dispute may drift towards acrimonious court proceedings. Alternatively, you may already feel ‘stuck’ in court proceedings that are moving very slowly and you believe this is damaging, financially or emotionally, for you and your family. Asking a neutral evaluator for their professional view on your situation might liberate you and {partner_name} from the stressful court process.

1.title: Hybrid Mediation
1.summary:
Hybrid mediation involves a neutral mediator assisting you and {partner_name} to discuss your differences and explore solutions. There are some crucial differences between a traditional mediation and a hybrid mediation. A hybrid mediation does not require you and {partner_name} to be in the same room.

You can have your own family lawyer in the room with you providing advice as the mediation progresses. A Hybrid mediator can hold confidences (respect confidential information provided to them by you or {partner_name}) if it helps to create an agreement. Agreements reached within hybrid mediation can usually be turned into legally binding documents because of the presence of lawyers supporting the mediation. Hybrid mediation can be used to solve issues relating to how to divide up any assets or how to organise child care arrangements.

1.title: Lawyer Negotiation
1.summary:
Lawyer negotiation is an appropriate option, {name}, if you and {partner_name} cannot sit in the same room as each other (like in a mediation or a collaborative setting). In this case, the communication between you and {partner_name} will mainly be letters or emails - by a lawyer on your behalf with another lawyer appointed by {partner_name}.

The lawyers will also have telephone discussions with each other. Sometimes, in order to negotiate an agreement, the lawyers may organise a ‘round table’ meeting so they can talk face-to-face. The lawyers will ask you and {partner_name} to be there although you would not need to be in the same room as each other unless you both agreed to it.

If agreement is reached the lawyers will draft up a consent order and get it approved by a family court by way of a ‘paper-work-only’ application - this means you do not need to go to court. If agreement cannot be reached by the lawyer negotiation route, or any other option, your lawyer will advise whether court proceedings are necessary.

1.title: One Lawyer One Couple
1.summary:
The ‘One Lawyer – One Couple’ option is an alternative to ‘lawyering up’ where opposing lawyers fight their own client’s corner. The One Lawyer model offers a single, neutral lawyer who will look after both of you, working hard in the best interests of your family.

It involves a series of meetings but, unlike mediation, your lawyer-neutral can offer advice to both you and {partner_name} and then deal with the drafting of any agreement into a court order. Some of the lawyers offering the One Lawyer model will work closely with a family consultant (usually a trained counsellor or therapist) to make sure that both of you feel fully supported during discussions. Other neutral experts, such as financial planners or accountants can be brought into the meetings if you and {partner_name} require holistic support.

one_lawyer_one_couple.affordability:
You pay for one neutral family lawyer who advises you and {partner_name} together, supports agreement through joint meetings, and prepares the final legally binding documents, submitting them to court if required. This avoids the cost of two separate lawyers. Additional neutral experts, such as a family consultant or financial specialist, are used only if both of you agree they add value.

This option is significantly cheaper than going to court, where separate lawyers, hearings, and delays drive up costs. It is usually more expensive than traditional mediation because the lawyer can provide legal advice and draft binding court documents. However, using one lawyer keeps costs lower than most lawyer-led processes and can reduce the risk of failed mediation, escalating conflict, and additional expense.

Legal Aid is not available so costs are usually self-funded and shared equally, with alternative contributions sometimes agreed where finances differ. If finances are tight, you may seek financial support from family or friends.

1.title: Arbitration
1.summary:
Arbitration is process where in an impartial legal expert, an arbitrator acts like a judge to provide a binding decision (sometimes called an ‘award’) on a dispute between you and {partner_name}. This is very different to mediation where an agreement is not binding upon you and {partner_name}.

An arbitrator can deal with financial disputes and with disagreements over your children. Unlike the family court, you and {partner_name} would be able to choose the arbitrator as well as the date and location of the arbitration. Arbitration can be arranged much more quickly than a court hearing and is usually less expensive. It is a good option to consider if you feel ‘stuck’ in court proceedings that are moving very slowly and you believe this is damaging, financially or emotionally, for you and your family.

arbitration.affordability:
You pay for an independent arbitrator, a specialist legal expert who makes a binding decision on specific disputes, similar to a judge but without court delays. You will also incur legal costs for your own solicitor to prepare evidence and submissions. Additional experts, such as accountants or child specialists, are used only where you and {partner_first_name} agree they add value and help resolve issues efficiently.

Arbitration is usually faster and less expensive than taking a case to a final court hearing, where costs can escalate through delay and multiple hearings.
